summary:
No state-level legal gender-recognition procedure is documented for Durango in the vetted sources, and none of the available reporting separates the state's own position from the national picture. Legal gender recognition in Mexico is established state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure by that date, that two further states operate one in practice without enactment, and that six legislatures have enacted nothing.

Recognition is narrower than the headline count suggests. Only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure across the federation. These rulings bind Durango even where its own legislature has not legislated.

The consequences of an absent or obstructive procedure are documented in detail. The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, examining a Mexican state with no recognition procedure, found that trans people there face violence, harassment and humiliation at every document request or appearance scrutiny, and are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions when their identity documents do not match their gender. The same reporting records identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Deadly violence sits above that administrative gap. Trans women continue to be killed with effective impunity: the Aug 2023 murder of Karina Gomez in Villahermosa, Tabasco, is one case carried in the record, and more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, with transfemicide impunity thought to be higher still. In July 2024 Mexico City's legislature passed the Paola Buenrostro law, making transfemicide punishable by up to 70 years; it is the second of the 32 states to criminalise the offence, after Nayarit, where the maximum sentence is 60 years.

For a visitor to Durango, the operative rule is the national framework, not any locally enacted procedure. The vetted sources do not identify Durango as the home of a recognition procedure, and they do not identify it among the six states lacking one either. What is verified is the country-wide pattern: formal rights that enforcement makes unreliable, and a documented gap between statute and practice.
tangentialFactors:
Recognition in Mexico is uneven by design. Two states operate a procedure without legislation and only seven states cover children, so a document obtained in one state may carry different weight in another. The Supreme Court's 2022 guidelines and the Inter-American Court's standard exist precisely because that patchwork leaves trans residents exposed wherever local administration is hostile or slow.

The Tabasco case is the reference example for what silence in state law produces on the ground: document requests become points of scrutiny, and trans people are pushed out of work, clinics, classrooms and banking while carrying papers that contradict their identity. Incidents recorded in Guanajuato show the same mechanism operating where the paperwork does not match the person.

Impunity is the strongest comparative marker. With more than 95% of Mexican homicides unpunished in 2022, and transfemicide impunity assessed as higher, the criminalisation of transfemicide is a trend rather than an established norm: Nayarit legislated first, Mexico City followed in July 2024 with a 70-year maximum. Whether Durango sits among the states that have not acted on this offence is not established in the available sources.
localsOnly:
Durango residents transacting with state authorities operate under the national framework even where their own legislature has not legislated. The Supreme Court's 2022 guidelines bind the states, and they extend legal gender recognition to minors, so an administrative refusal cannot rest on the absence of a state statute alone.

Where no local procedure exists, residents are the group documented as losing access: employment, health services, education and financial transactions all fall away when identity documents do not match a person's gender. The record shows this happening in Mexican states without procedures, and shows no Durango-specific enforcement pattern to confirm or contradict the national finding.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Durango is one of the six states whose legislature has enacted no legal gender-recognition procedure is unresolved. The March 2025 count establishes that six states fall into that category but does not name them in the sources available for this record.

No Durango-specific enforcement data is sourced: nothing verifies how Durango's authorities process name-and-gender petitions, whether local police practise document scrutiny, or how quickly cases are resolved. Local incidents, prosecutions and institutional practice remain unverified rather than absent.

The record also does not resolve whether Durango has enacted its own transfemicide statute, or whether victims in the state fall under national homicide law alone. The two jurisdictions named in the sources are Nayarit and Mexico City, and no claim about Durango's position on this offence is supported.
